title: The alchemist's elixir
hookLine: fix yourself first, or start helping as you are? two Buddhist answers, and an elixir
tomorrow: wanting to help, and helping. what's the gap?

cards: Every self-help shelf says the same thing a hundred ways: put your own oxygen mask on first. Get your life in order, then help others. It sounds wise, and it often is.
Shantideva's poem says something that sounds like the opposite. Old alchemists dreamed of an elixir that turns base metal into gold. The wish to wake up for everyone, he says, is that elixir.
It takes this ordinary body and turns it into something priceless. Not after you're fixed. Now.

teach.h: THE ELIXIR: THE WISH TO WAKE FOR ALL.
teach.b: Two real voices inside Buddhism, and each deserves its best case. First, Shantideva. The awakening mind, bodhicitta, is the wish to become awake for the sake of all beings.
He calls it the finest alchemist's elixir: it takes this impure body and makes it into the priceless form of a Buddha. A verse earlier he goes further.
The moment that wish arises, even someone stuck in the prison of suffering is called a child of the Buddhas. His point: you don't wait to be gold before you start.
The elixir works on base metal. That's what it's for.

teach.h: THE OTHER VOICE: TRAIN YOURSELF FIRST.
teach.b: Now the other voice, which many teachers lean on. The Dhammapada says, in its own way, set yourself first in what is right, and only then teach others.

Elsewhere it warns against neglecting your own good for someone else's, however great. Its best case: a drowning person can't pull anyone out. Train the mind first, or your help gets tangled with your own anger and need.
Here's where they meet. Shantideva's next chapters are mostly about guarding your own mind. And the Dhammapada's road is full of kindness.

teach.h: BOTH KEEP BOTH; THEY ARGUE ORDER.
teach.b: The argument is about the order, and both keep both.

how: In Mahayana communities, a practice session often opens by recalling the wish to awaken for the benefit of all beings; Theravada teachers often stress training one's own mind, with kindness for others built into that training.

o: the wish to wake for all, turning ordinary into priceless
a secret potion monks drink to live for a very long time
a medicine that cures every illness of the body

games.q: two voices, one argument — tap the pairs.
p: the wish to wake up for all beings
start now: it works on base metal
set yourself in what is right first

s: in Shantideva's poem, you must be pure before the awakening mind can arise
he says the moment it arises, even someone in the prison of suffering is called a child of the Buddhas.
the Dhammapada tells you to set yourself in what is right before teaching others
it's the other voice in today's argument, and it has a strong case.
the two views mean one side doesn't care about others and the other doesn't train the mind
both keep both. Shantideva spends chapters on guarding the mind; the Dhammapada's road is full of kindness.

games.q: your study group argues: help a struggling friend now, or sort out your own mess first? you're on Shantideva's side. what's the other side's best case?
o: a drowning person can't pull anyone out; help tangled with your own anger can hurt.
helping others is a distraction, so it's better to avoid it until you're done training.
other people's problems aren't your business, so there's no need to step in.
games.why: that's the strongest form of the Dhammapada's view: train the mind so your help is clean. Shantideva's reply: the elixir works on base metal, so start as you are, and keep training.

practice: Take a pen and write one small thing you'll do today that helps someone besides you. Then, under it, write one thing that keeps your own mind steady while you do it. Read both lines back once, and sit quietly with the page.

wordCard.voice: The alchemist's elixir: Shantideva's picture of the awakening mind. Poured on base metal, it makes gold, starting with whoever you are today.

orig.note: Sanskrit: bodhi, awakening, and citta, mind: the mind set on awakening for the sake of all beings.

carryVoice: Here's the line: base metal to gold, and nobody starts as gold. Four days into the poem; see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 1.9-1.10 (the moment it arises, one is called a child of the Buddhas; the awakening mind as the finest alchemical elixir)
Dhammapada 158 and 166 (set yourself first in what is right; do not neglect your own good for another's)
